say: Tokyo's subway carries over eight million rides a day. And the whole thing started with one guy... and two pockets full of beans.
In 1914, a businessman named Noritsugu Hayakawa rode the London Underground and thought, Tokyo needs this. Back home, the streets were jammed with crowded trams.
To prove people would ride it, he stood at busy corners counting traffic. A white bean in his left pocket for every person walking by. A black bean in his right for every car.
He started his subway company in 1920. Then in 1923 the Great Kanto earthquake hit, money dried up, and the digging didn't start until 1925.
So he shrank the plan. Instead of crossing the city, the first line was just two point two kilometers, from Ueno to Asakusa.
It opened on December thirtieth, 1927, as the first subway in Asia. More than forty thousand people rode it that first morning, and some waited over two hours.
The line kept growing, to Shimbashi in 1934 and Shibuya in 1939. That's today's orange Ginza Line. After the war, new lines followed, one after another.
Today there are thirteen lines and about two hundred eighty six stations. The deepest one, Roppongi on the Oedo Line, sits about forty two meters underground.
And that first little line from Ueno to Asakusa? It's still running. It turns one hundred years old on December thirtieth, 2027.
